utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There are some decisions that I'd like to give. First, in relation to the question of time for examination-in-chief, cross-examination, the Prosecution will be given 30 minutes for examination-in-chief of 92 bis or 92 ter witnesses, unless the testimony relates to a witness who is a combination of 92 bis/ter evidence and viva voce evidence. The time to be allocated to the Defence for cross-examination of 92 bis and 92 ter witnesses will be based on several factors, including an evaluation of the significance of the witness's testimony, the original estimate of the Prosecutor of the time required as provided in the 65 ter list, the length of the witness's prior statement, and the number of exhibits to be tendered through the witness. In order to facilitate the parties in their preparation, the Chamber will review the list of witnesses for the week follow and based on the factors mentioned will set times for the examination and cross-examination of each scheduled witness. The parties will be notified of these times. The Prosecution is requested to be as precise as possible in its estimates. In all cases, the parties may make an application for variation of the time periods set. Now, on Monday, the 12th of February, the Prosecution sought to admit into evidence a document with a 65 ter number 02287. This is a report by Kemal Buco, concerning a sniping incident on the 23rd November 1994, discussed with that witness on the 2nd of February, 2007. The Prosecution had at that time inadvertently omitted to seek the admission of this document into evidence. The Trial Chamber hereby admits this report, 65 ter number 02287 into evidence. On the 5th of February, the Prosecution filed a motion for admission of the written statement of witness John Jordan, pursuant to Rule 92 ter. The Defence responded yesterday that it had no objection to the Prosecution's request. The Trial Chamber hereby grants the Prosecution motion and admits the witness statement of John Jordan into evidence upon fulfillment of the conditions set out in Rule 92 ter. The Trial Chamber notes that the time originally estimated for this witness's testimony was three hours and that the Prosecution estimates that as a partial Rule 92 ter and partial viva voce witness, the estimated time required will be two hours. The Trial Chamber also notes the significance of the testimony of this witness and the number of exhibits intended to be tendered. The Trial Chamber will allow one hour for the examination-in-chief and one and a quarter hour for cross-examination subject to an application for more time should either party consider that necessary. Now, I understand that a party had a matter to be raised. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's not us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Not you. Mr. Tapuskovic, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this issue is of great importance. Perhaps it is the most important issue out of all of the problems that the Defence faces, and it relates precisely to the issue of translation of our documents. Our Defence team has not yet gained access to the CLSS to the translation service to this day, and although we wanted to get some documents even before the beginning of trial, we still have no access to the translation service. We have already omitted to confront some witnesses with some documents. Now, in the period that follows, I am facing a very difficult problem. Mr. Whiting is showering me with e-mails from which it transpires that presenting documents in B/C/S is absolutely unacceptable. And many months may pass before I get my documents translated. I really need you to appreciate this problem, and I will try to minimise the number of documents that I present in B/C/S. I have very important documents for foreign observers and foreign commanders that concern issues that I have tried to reserve so far, because they haven't been translated yet. If it is impossible to get these translations from the service that is working for us and for you, then something has to be done. All last afternoon I had to deal with e-mail messages from Mr. Whiting instead of preparing for the hearing. Some documents are in B/C/S, they were not presented in a timely manner, and they were accessible to the Prosecution at the time that the witness concerned took a solemn oath. It was a mountain of papers that I had to deal with, and I received them the day before the witness appeared. Your Honours, all I'm asking for is equal treatment and a correct attitude. Maybe in our Defence case I will find myself in the shoes that Mr. Whiting is in now. But when Mr. Whiting does not show a certain witness a single document, I have to show him a number of documents. That's -- we have to deal with this problem and that's the only thing that I'm really interested in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll consider that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This actually touches on a problem which is very serious for us. I was going to raise it after the direct examination, and it has a problem that has several parts to it, only one of which has been identified by Defence counsel. I think it is a bit of an exaggeration that I showered Defence counsel with e-mails. It was just four e-mails about the exhibits, and there are actually two issues. The first is that we are receiving these long lists of exhibits to be used in cross-examination that are not translated. The list I received for this witness has 15 documents that are not translated, that are in B/C/S. That, obviously, causes us serious difficulty in preparing for -- it's really no use in preparing for the cross-examination or any possible re-examination if we're running around trying to figure out what the documents say. I don't know what the problem is behind that. I don't know when it was requested that these documents be translated. I don't know what the issues are, but it's also not apparent to me that many of these documents are of particular relevance to this particular witness. Nearly all of them are military documents, and this is a policeman but that is for Defence counsel to resolve. There is a second part to this, and that is that-- and this has happened more than once and it happened on this occasion. We're getting a list shortly after the witness begins testifying, and that's what happened yesterday. I got a list. I stayed here last night, looking at the documents, preparing. This morning I got a completely new list and from the new list four documents have been dropped, and there were 13 new documents on it. And all of these, again, in B/C/S, so I have to prepare all over again. And that has happened on more than one occasion. That happened with witness Fraser. Midway through, we received another list doubling the amount of documents. I had understood the Rule to be that we would receive the list of documents at the -- when the witness began testifying, with the understanding that if something arose during the direct examination, another document might become relevant. It seems surprising to go me that so many documents are relevant during the examination and also, you know, this problem about untranslated documents. We would object generally to witnesses being shown documents in B/C/S that we do not have a translation for. There may be -- may be exceptions to that where it is necessary. If it happens once, once in a while, okay, I understand that. But to receive 13 -- 15 documents which are in B/C/S, that, in our view, is not workable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If it's a very short document, the practice has been to put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, the problem is that these are not necessarily short documents; and then with the 15 of them, the accumulation is that they are not short. And also we need to see -- Defence counsel in a number of cases already in this trial has just read out one sentence of a document, and the issue becomes clarified in another part of the document; or when it is put into context, it takes on a different meaning. And so we need to be able to understand what the entire document says. The only way we can do that is if we have a translation of it. We can handle it if it happens once in a while. We can sit down with an interpreter. But if it is 15 documents for a small witness like this, happening routinely, that becomes unimaginable. We do not have the resources to translate all the Defence documents while the witness is testifying and trying to prepare for that. That is impossible; we can't do that. And it's not fair to the Prosecution that documents are being shown to a witness that we cannot understand, that we don't understand what they mean. That's not fair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. [Trial Chamber confers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, there's the two problems that have been identified by the parties. The first is the problem encountered by the Defence in having its documents translated sufficiently speedily for the purposes for which they require them. We've had this problem in other cases. It's not a new problem. I will cause an investigation to be made with the CLSS and have the CLSS present a status report on the documents submitted by the Defence in this case for translation, so that status report. And I would like the court deputy to note this because it's the court deputy who will transmit this instruction to the CLSS. The status report from the CLSS will tell us how many documents have been presented; the volume, the pages, and the precise stage that they are at in the translation. Of course, the time when they were presented is important. But here I'd like both parties to note that the documents to be presented for translation should be as brief as possible and should really be confined to those areas that are relevant to the purposes for which they are sought. There's no point presenting for translation a 20- or 30-page document when you're only going to rely on one or two pages in it. So I'd like the parties to note that. The second problem raised is the time when the parties notify the other party and the Chamber of the documents to be used in examination-in-chief and cross-examination, and we had made a ruling on this and we intend to apply the ruling strictly and both parties are to note this. But the problem raised by Mr. Whiting is more applicable to the -- to the Defence in this case; and the ruling that we made was that at the beginning of examination-in-chief, the Defence is to notify the Prosecution and the Chamber of the documents that it will use in cross-examination. And I have it precisely here. It orders the Defence to provide the Prosecution, the Registry, and the Trial Chamber with a list of exhibits it intends to use in court during cross-examination at the commencement of the examination-in-chief of that witness and after he or she has made the solemn declaration pursuant to Rule 90 (A) of the Rules. So that once that time has passed, strictly speaking, no change or addition should be made to that list of documents notified; at any rate, not without the leave of the Trial Chamber. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I was probably not clear enough. To this day, the Defence team has no electronic access to translation. We have met all the requirements. We have filled in all the forms. We have done all that is necessary to again, but we have to electronic access to the translation service. That is one thing. Second, Your Honours, we have tendered all the evidence, and all of it was accessible to the Prosecutor at the moment when the witness took oath. That is the most important thing. In addition, if you allow me, I can reduce my cross-examination to two briefest documents that the Prosecutor has had for two years now. The Prosecutor mentions 13 or 14 documents, but most of them were only a half page long. I really took care about this. So far, the Prosecutor has never once found himself in a situation where he has to deal with evidence that we did not supply in advance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Explain to me what is meant by "not having any electronic access to translation." What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Somebody more expert could explain that to you. It's just that the documents that we presented, we're not able to be included in the electronic translation system. I really can't explain this to you, because my only grasp of this -- these things is not very good. Anyway, I'm told that we have no access to the TTS system. We have documents that we have prepared. We have filled in the proper forms, and we cannot place this -- these documents into the TTS system, as far as my colleagues have explained to me. And if they are not in this TTS system, they can't be translated. It has to do with this new system that is introduced. We had to invest an enormous effort for our documents to enter this TTS system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Does that mean that the CLSS would not have received the documents that you wish to have translated?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am honestly telling you, I don't understand these things. They did not give us access to this system. I went to see the chief of that service directly. I have all of the documents ready. I can give them to that service this very moment, but it's a system that doesn't function if you don't log in. I'm honestly telling you, I don't understand this at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me consult with my colleagues, because they have a better understanding than I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, then, the problem is not with the CLSS. It is that you're saying you -- you have no access, electronic access to the system. So the CLSS has not received the documents, indeed, you haven't been able to send them. Well, I think what we'll have to about done is that I will instruct you to consult with the court deputy, who should have at his disposal the services of the technical staff to resolve that problem. Well, Mr. Tapuskovic, if you have had this problem all along, I'm surprised that you're only raising it now, because we're about five, six weeks into the trial now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would note that it's only being raised because I complained about it, because I complained in these e-mails, and I told the counsel that I was going to raise this today. We find it a little distressing to learn now that this has been an ongoing problem, and it hasn't been addressed. It hasn't been raised, only when we complain about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't want to justify myself or to defend myself. I told you earlier that my greatest problem was to receive the documents that I had selected in the archives of Bosnia-Herzegovina sometime ago where I worked. For half a year, I was almost living in those archives. And only 15 days after the beginning of the trial on the 2nd of February, I received finally the documents. I went to see the chief of the translation service directly, and I addressed them very courteously to discuss the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: My instruction remains the same. You are to be in touch with the court deputy immediately after the session ends, and the court deputy tomorrow will avail himself of the services of the technical staff and have this problem resolved and report to me by the beginning of the session tomorrow. And I am to say that the session tomorrow will take place in Courtroom III, in Courtroom III. Well, let us have the witness brought in.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, while the witness is being brought in, I just wanted to say that exhibit 65 ter number 02287, which was submitted pursuant to your oral decision, will become Exhibit P112.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir. When we stopped yesterday, you told us about an occasion in the Autumn of 1994 when you were investigating a shelling at the Holiday Inn. You were on top of the National Restaurant and sniping came from the direction of Grbavica. I just had one last question. What was the weather like on that occasion, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was cloudy, sort of. It was raining, as a matter of fact not right at the time. But it was cloudy and foggy, the way it can be in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, I'm going to ask you some questions about an event that occurred at Cobanija Street number 7, on the 16th of June 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: For your benefit, Your Honours, this is scheduled incident number 13, shelling incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, did you investigate an incident that occurred on that date at that location?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What happened there? What were you investigating?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a shelling, and the boiler room that heated those buildings on that street was hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, did -- to your knowledge, did Cobanija Street have another name before it was called Cobanija Street?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It used to be called -- well, the name escapes me right now, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If I said a name, might it refresh your recollection?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the street name Tome Masarika?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Tome Masarika; that's what it was called.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That was the name of Cobanija Street in the past, before the war?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we see 65 ter exhibit 213, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's the report that I compiled and completed, the on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, under point 4 of the report, it gives -- it states the direction that the highly destructive projectile was fired from. Can you tell what it says there, what direction?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says that it flew in from a north-easterly direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. I would note from the Trial Chamber and Defence counsel, there is a mistake on the English translation of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, did you review other reports and documents concerning this event which talked about the direction that the projectile came from?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Whiting, what is the mistake that -- is it north-west?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. What it actually says is north-east in the B/C/S. There's a mistake in the translation. The witness just testified what it was in B/C/S, and it was translated as north-east.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I'm just a little concerned because the directions are quite important in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's -- I'm happy to have it confirmed and reviewed, but it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'd like to have it confirmed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's fine. We can submit it to CLSS to have it reviewed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: They can just look at the B/C/S and tell us what the what the --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's fine. That's what I tried to do. The witness read what it says in the report, and it was translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us have the interpreter give us the translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter can confirm what Mr. Whiting has just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be of assistance. It does say north-east. That is precisely what it says in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, did you review other reports regarding this incident where a similar translation errors were made with respect to the direction?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I looked at my own photofiles, and there were some mistranslations there. It was the photo files that I compiled. It was supposed to say north-east, but I think the translation actually read north-west which was erroneous.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In all of the reports that you reviewed regarding this incident, was the direction -- in the B/C/S language, was the direction always identified as north-east, as it is here in this report?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We should go through all these documents, each and every one of them. We can't speak in general terms like this. We do realise that an error was made in this particular incident, but I'm not sure which other documents Mr. Whiting has in mind. I think he should just display the whole lot to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to put all of the documents into evidence, and we can review it later. I don't think it's worthwhile to spend the time to go through --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No. I don't think it's necessary to review them individually. Of course, the -- the Defence may make a reference in cross-examination to any of them --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- If it has a doubt about the accuracy of the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vidovic, do you know how it was determined that the projectile came from the north-east?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was based on the point of impact where the projectile hit the boiler room. That's what indicated the direction from which the missile had arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did the investigation determine what the projectile was that struck the boiler room on that day?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Later investigations were carried out, which ascertained that the projectile in question had been an air bomb.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know who in particular made that determination; that is, which group, and how they made that determination. What was it based on?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bits of the projectile were collected and submitted for analysis to the KDZ department in what used to be the state ministry of the interior, which is the federal ministry of interior now. Their own experts conducted analysis. I'm not sure which specific methods they used.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know if witnesses were able to provide any information which contributed to the determination that this was an air bomb?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. According to witness statements, it produced a very peculiar sound during its flight. The way they described it, it sounded very much like a lorry flying through the air.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Have you, yourself, ever seen an air bomb, an unexploded air bomb?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I've seen one on one occasion. It had been brought over from someplace or other. It was unexploded. It was taken apart and simply left behind near the building in which I worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know where it came from? You said it was unexploded. Where did it come from?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly where it came from, where it was found, or where it landed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let me put my question a little differently. Do you know if this air bomb that you saw came from the -- the Serb army, or did it come from the Bosnian army, or do you not know?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't from the Bosnian army. It was most probably fired by the Serb side. One thing I do know is that it was entirely cracked up by the time it reached us, because it had landed already and smashed against the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So just I'm clear about your testimony, this was an air bomb that was launched and landed and it was smashed. It was damaged, but it had not exploded. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Trial Chamber what it looked like. What does an air bomb look like; or at least the one that you saw, what did it look like?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I remember, it was made up of two component parts. One of the components was made up of four rockets or what I assume to have been rockets, and the other part was made up of the air bomb proper. In my estimate, it could have weighed anywhere between 200 and 250 kilos. It's difficult to tell just by looking at it. It looked quite big, and the two component parts were welded together.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How big were the rockets?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my estimate, two, maybe three metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now going back to the report that you wrote --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, the witness should be asked why he concluded that the air bomb came from the Serbian side and not from the Bosnian side. Why did you say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that was what I was told by my colleagues. I had asked them how the bomb came to be there in the first place. I simply wanted to the know who had done it, what exactly occurred and how it got to be there in the first place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, going back to this report that you wrote, does the report indicate wether anyone was injured in this air bomb attack on this date?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this case, on Cobanija Street, three persons were injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And the names are indicated there on the report.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the names are there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this document be admitted, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As P113, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could we please look at 65 ter 2872. It's the map of Sarajevo. And if we could zoom into the right-hand part of the map where the river is, just below the river on the right-hand side. If you can zoom in -- do that again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, you're going to know this map better than I do. Can you see Cobanija Street on there, or do we need to zoom in some more?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we can zoom in between Skenderija and Bistrik. There we go, perfect.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could the witness be given the pen to mark where it is, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And if you could mark where -- where, to the best of your recollection, this occurred, Cobanija Street 7, on the map?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. The witness has drawn a dot and a circle around it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, were there any military facilities near this location, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you know how far the closest military facility was to this location, in terms of metres or even kilometres or ...

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I'm sorry, but I can't say. The only military facility that I can remember right now was the headquarters at Bistrik, but that's where UNPROFOR was stationed at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you put an X where that was.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks] Around about here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. And you said that it was a boiler room that was struck and I think also some garages. Was that -- is that part of a residential complex or building?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This entire section of Cobanija Street is residential.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: To your -- did you learn in your investigation if there were any military -- any soldiers present at the location when it was hit by the air bomb?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not that I heard of.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this be made an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be admitted as Exhibit P214, also a registry correction. The last two exhibits were admitted as P112 and 113. They should have been 212 and 213.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could look at 65 ter Exhibit 136, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, do you recognise this document, or can you tell us what this document is?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do recognise it. As far as I can tell, this is the header. This is the first part of the expert analysis of part of part of the projectile that landed on Cobanija Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity to review this document before coming into court today?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: From its appearance, does it appear to you based on your experience to be an authentic document?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this be admitted into evidence, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P215, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we look at exhibit 65 ter 138, please. I don't think we need the -- well, no, that's fine. Are you going to put up the translation. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recognise this, Mr. Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are photographs that I took at the actual site, Cobanija Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did you write the captions?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we look at the picture at the top, so it's the first picture on this first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I refer to as the boiler room, the one that was hit by the projectile, and you can see the exact point of impact where it smashed against the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honours, these colour Xeroxes are actually pretty good with the captions. I do -- if it's assistance to either the Trial Chamber or the Defence counsel, I do have a set of -- a printed version of these photographs, if it is of any assistance. But I would ask that these photographs be admitted into evidence along with their captions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P216, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we look at exhibit 65 ter 122, please, and if we could go to page 2 of the B/C/S and page 1 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, can you tell us what this report is?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the official report compiled by officials of the crime squad, those who carried out the on-site investigation at Cobanija Street. Another thing that I can see here is that all of the incidents that occurred on that day are described in this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you have an opportunity also to review this report before coming into court today. And, same question, does it appear to you, based on your experience, to be an authentic report?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have seen this report before. I saw it before I came into the courtroom, and I believe that this is an authentic document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this be admitted into evidence, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P217, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we look, please, at exhibit 65 ter 137.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you tell us what this is?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can tell, this is a hospital document. I believe that this is a medical finding of some kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I gave up objecting several times in a row, but this is something for an expert. This is for a medical expert. It's a medical document. We can hardly expect a witness who is not familiar with that field to establish the authenticity of this document. Perhaps a doctor could. A while ago, we had another document where expertise would have been required. He is a witness, but he certainly is no expert, and I think you should take the matter in hand, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, let me hear from Mr. Whiting on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm no going ask the witness to comment on or interpret the document at all. He is not an expert. He is not a doctor. I don't think he would be qualified to do that. I'm simply going to ask him if it is familiar to him as a medical document from the time, from the area, from -- and authenticate it that way and put it into evidence. I think that -- in our view, that is sufficient authentication for it to go into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is precisely the problem that I think we're facing. I don't think the witness is able to do that. I don't think he can confirm the time the document was produced. We all see that; nobody is trying to challenge that. But the Prosecutor is asking him to also confirm the substance of the document as well as the signature that it bears and whatever else it's about. If it's just about the date being confirmed, in that case, I have no reason to oppose this. [Trial Chamber confers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, what is the value to you of this document? The witness can't speak to its substance.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, if the document is in evidence, the document largely speaks for itself about the injuries that were suffered by the victims of the air bomb on that day. The victims are identified in the report, and these are medical records of what occurred to the victims. They largely speak for themselves, and I can't imagine there is really any dispute about what the injuries are in this case. And if there is, if there's a dispute about what the injuries are, we can take it up with other witnesses. But that's -- I cannot imagine that is a point of contention. This is not a sniping case where the injuries might indicate something about the case itself. [Trial Chamber confers].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll mark it for identification. Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I know a bit of Latin, and I have forgotten a lot. All of these are Latin terms. How have a witness, who is testifying only as a witness, say anything --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have ruled. We'll mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be marked for identification as P218.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, this may require -- for one thing, the exhibit should have six pages in it. While there are Latin terms, there are other explanations that are not in Latin. If we're going to need another witness to get this sort of evidence into evidence, these sorts of documents, obviously, we're going to have to add witnesses, doctors, and medical experts. I wouldn't think that is necessary, but maybe this is something that we can resolve with Defence counsel. As I said, I can't imagine that these injuries are really a point of contention in the case, but I will move on. If we could lock at 65 ter Exhibit 733, please, and if we could go to page 6 of the B/C/S and page 1 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is, again, a report of mine concerning an on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: For the benefit of Your Honours, this is now about a separate, different incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What's the date that this occurred and what, briefly speaking, what happened?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It happened on the 14th of February, 1995 in Zmaja od Bosne Street when a tram going from Bascarsija towards the depot at Alipasin Pole was shot at. One passenger was injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Does the report indicate the direction from which the fire came?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It says the shot came from the south-east.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And do you recall how that was determined?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was the determined based on eye-witness reports on the basis of the direction in which the tram was moving and the damage inflicted on the tram.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In addition to this document that you wrote, did you have an opportunity to review several other documents pertaining to this incident that were together with this document, and did those documents appear authentic to you?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have seen some other documents, and I believe that it is authentic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could this exhibit be marked and put into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be admitted as Exhibit P219.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could we look at 65 ter Exhibit 1170, please, and if we could go to page 4 of the B/C/S and page 1 of the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This is sniping incident number what?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry. This is an unscheduled incident, the last one and this one, and they are not dropped incidents. They were always unscheduled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But have we heard other witnesses on this incident before?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Not my knowledge, but I could be mistaken about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Will we be hearing other evidence on this unscheduled incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I can't say for certain, but perhaps not. And it's part -- part of the Prosecution to put in reports of unscheduled incidents, which, taken together, support the counts in the indictment. Not -- obviously, with respect to every unscheduled incident, we cannot call the victims and all of the witnesses and so forth. But we will put in investigative reports which contain that kind of information, as does this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise this report?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It's another of my reports from an on-site investigation, in this case, of a shelling incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what is the date of this incident and where did it occur?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 11th of July, 1995, in Omla Dinska Street.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic is on his feet. Mr. Tapuskovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This incident that we are dealing with now, is it also covered by the indictment as one of the scheduled incidents?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This is not a scheduled incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's unscheduled, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Again, in connection with this incident, did you review other reports before coming to court today, and were you able to determine whether those reports appeared authentic to you?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I have seen some other documents and they appear authentic to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tapuskovic, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I really cannot understand this line of questioning. If the intention is to speak of some documents that he has seen, the witness, then we should all look at them together. He was just asked whether he has seen some other documents and whether he can confirm their accuracy; that's something that I have never encountered my practice before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, I think that will be a matter for you to -- to raise in your cross-examination, if you -- if you think it will go to the credibility of the witness, the witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. It's merely to establish that there are other documents that pertain to these incidents which, of course, have been disclosed to the Defence, and the Defence is well aware of them. Could this document be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P220, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Can I just ask the witness -- could we have Exhibit P217 back on the screen, and I apologise in the being quick enough to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, for some reason, although your microphone was on, it was hard to hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I will ask you again, if I could ask you to bring become Exhibit P217, which was the crime squad report of 17 June, 1995. And as I said, I apologise for not being quick enough to react while it was on the screen in front of us. But it disappeared so quickly, so I thought I should wait with my question. And my question is: While we're waiting for the document to reappear, that I thought I saw that in the report the direction was given as coming from north-west and not from north-east as we had just established. And I want to verify this and bring it up with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, you will recall that with this exhibit that the witness testified that it was about -- that this exhibit covered a number of incidents on that date, and so that may be the source of the confusion. The --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes. You see in the last paragraph: "A survey of the scene confirmed that a modified aircraft bomb was fired from the aggressive position," so the north-west on the 16th of June. It may be that this is not referring to the same incident as the one in which we established that the bomb was fired from north-east, but I thought it was, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: There's one at 1000 hours and that's not the same one, and I don't know -- and that is north-west. But if we turn to the second page in the English, and I don't know about the B/C/S, the first -- no. We have to go to the top of the document. The first paragraph refers to our incident, and there it does say north-west. And there we could ask, again, the witness, it's -- if we can find it in the B/C/S and give the translation -- yes. It's midway in the page on the B/C/S, where it says 16th at 1710 hours and then -- and the witness can read the direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Could the witness please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If he can read it, if he can see it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Should I read it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Yes, please. Because I would like to know where did the bomb actually come from. Was it north-east or was it north-west?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see here it's written from north-west, but in my report it says north-east.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: That's what I want to bring up. Because now I think -- you know, the Chamber needs to be reassured where did the bomb come from and can we be shown on the map where that was, who held the territory in the north-east or north-west. How are we to ascertain which side fired this bomb? Can you please assist us, Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, we can go back to 65 ter 2872, the map. And while that is coming up --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'll ask this: Mr. Vidovic, you reviewed your reports and other reports related to this incident. Now that it's been drawn to your attention that in this report it identifies the direction as north-west, does that cause you to change in any way what you put -- what you represented in your report that it came from the north-east?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not change anything, especially now that I'm thinking about it. This axis, north-east, leads to a crack between buildings; and to the north-west, the entire area is densely built up and the bullet would sooner hit one of those buildings than go this way here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let me see if I can -- if I'm clear about what you're saying. Are you saying that given where the bomb hit, its point of impact, and the layout of the buildings around it and the openings around it, that it -- it -- that causes you to determine that it came from the north-east as opposed to the north-west. Because if it had come from the north-west, it would have hit another building before hitting this point. Is that your testimony? Did I clarify it?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. It was the bomb squad team that determined the direction from which the projectile came, also on the basis of the location of the impact. At the time there were also military observers present on the on-site investigation, and they determined the direction where it came from to be north-east as I wrote in my report. And this is -- what I recently mentioned is also one of the ways in which you can determine where it came from.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And the report that His Honour Judge Harhoff showed you a moment ago, which is Exhibit 217, P217, that is a report that summarized, as you testified, all of the incidents that occurred that day. How is -- do you know how such a report is prepared?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose that the report was drafted at the end of the day. The colleague who was writing it at the end of the day and after all the on-site investigations were performed for the day simply wrote an aggregate report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So it's an aggregate report which is written after the investigative reports are written, is that a fair summary of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, I'll ask then if we could look at the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could zoom in again on that location on the right-hand side, and it's between Skenderija and Bistrik. That might be good.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Are you able to see, Mr. Vidovic, where -- okay. There you can certainly see. Can you take the pen, mark again where the point of impact was and the direction that you believe it came from. Are you able to do that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks] .

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, just so the record is clear, the witness has drawn a dot with a circle around it and an arrow pointing to the upper right of the map. Now, sir, is it in your capacity to provide any information to the Trial Chamber about where the air bomb was fired from, or are you only able to tell the Trial Chamber the direction that it came from?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could only say the direction. I don't know the exact location.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- I think I have exhausted this subject with the witness. But if there are further questions you'd like me to address, I'm happy to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: No, not as far as the witness is concerned. He can testify no longer than this, but you would still need to persuade the Chamber that it was fired from either one or the other position-- side.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, you will recall that it's the Prosecution's position that only the, and there's been evidence on this, that only the Bosnian Serb army had these weapons. And that the -- the Bosnian army did not have these weapons. But before we move on and before it gets lost, could just mark this -- unless further markings are required on this map, I would ask that it be made an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P221, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we keep this on the system; it would help us a lot. I would refer to the last exhibit, P220. We have spoken of the shelling on the street of Cobanija, on Cobanija Street number 7, on the 11th of July, 1995, you said that the sound came from the north-west, the bomb came from the north-west. Obviously, you understand that we wish to understand who is responsible for this shelling in order to establish who is responsible. And if there has been shelling, what sort of bomb was used or shell was used. I would, therefore, like to know what sort of shell was used in this incident concerning Exhibit 220. This is my first question. Could you say what sort of a shell it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot say that exactly now, because we collected pieces of the projectile and forwarded -- forwarded them for expertise, and the expertise later established which projectile it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And do you know now what sort of a shell it may have been?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I remember, it was a mortar shell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And how did you reach the conclusion that the shell came from the north-west? And another question: Your conclusion or your report, was it corroborate the by other reports such as the reports of the UNMOs, for instance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not the one who determined on-site the direction where it came from. It was the whole team, especially the bomb squad team; plus in addition to my report, there was also a judge present, an investigating judge present from the Sarajevo district court. I think there is a report from the investigating judge. Otherwise, I don't think UN observers were present on this particular site.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is where you will be particularly helpful for the Chamber, as an expert, specialist of these matters. According to you, what -- which forces would be responsible for this shelling? Do you have a way of knowing or not? What forces, what army, what group would be responsible for this shelling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can only say what we determined at the on-site investigation; namely, which direction it was fired from. Further expertise to determine the location and the position is something that I cannot speak to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Thank you. I don't need the map anymore. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, you told Mr. Whiting that a colleague wrote an aggregate report based on all the on-site investigations. Would you plain explain what is meant by an aggregate report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That would be his daily report, his report for the day. In addition to that, he writes a report for each particular incident, and this daily report is forwarded on for information. So in addition, there should be an individual report for each incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. There is an individual report and an aggregate report. Now, in the aggregate report, it is stated the direction from which the fire came, from which the weapon came. Now, would that mean that the direction identified in the aggregate report reflects the direction stated in all the individual reports or perhaps only some of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only some of them. If you mean what is written in that part of the text, that particular bit relates only to one incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The conclusion in the aggregate report as to the direction from which the weapon was fired, what I'm asking is whether that direction is the direction that would be identified in all the individual on-site reports. So that if it said north-west in the aggregate report, did it say north-west in all the individual on-site investigations or perhaps in -- in nine out of ten, it said north-west; and in another one, it might have said north-east. That is what I'm trying to ascertain.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It should be, in relation it that incident, one, and not all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, just following up on President Robinson's question, as I understand was the case in this particular report, if there is a difference between what is written in the actual incident report, first, and then in the aggregate report at the end of the day, if there's a difference between these two report, which I understand there was- in the incident report, it said that it came from the north-east and in the aggregate, certainly, it says that the bomb was fired from the north-west, which of the two findings would then be passed on to -- to the next step in the -- in the procedures, I mean, in the reports that went on to the headquarters? No, you don't understand my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: There is, obviously, a difference in the two reports.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Which of the two findings would be -- which one prevails?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's difficult to say. If you ask me, both are equally important. I don't know where the error was made as far as my colleague who wrote down north-west was concerned. What I learned on the spot I wrote down immediately in my own report. That's as much as I can say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, it's -- I see. No, we are beyond the time for the break. So we'll take the break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If I may, and Defence counsel has no objection; I asked them. If I may just put a few more questions to the witness, it's in aim of trying to further clarify this issue about north-west, north-east.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Could we look at Exhibit P215, and if we could have the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vidovic, you testified earlier about this exhibit, that it was the ballistics or the bomb squad expert report; do you recall?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And are you able to -- well, now we've --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. We've lost the English. It's being flipped. .

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to draw your attention to, I think it's the third paragraph after -- it's -- and do you see on this document, what direction does this document say the projectile was fired from?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: North, north-east -- north-west.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: North, north-west. It's in the third paragraph. It's translated -- in the translation, it's north-west. It doesn't have north, it just says north-west. So, now -- now, we have -- your report said north-east. This bomb squad expert report says north, north-west. The aggregate report said north-west. Which -- which would -- which report in your mind --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see Mr. Tapuskovic on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I can tell, in the B/C/S, it doesn't say north, north-west -- my mistake, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So if I could put my question again. Your report, your on-site investigation report says north-east. This bomb squad expert analysis report says north, north-west, and the aggregate report says north-west. Which of those reports should prevail? Which is the better report or are you unable to say.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The expert analysis --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't think this is a proper question. It's not proper to ask this witness to assess this. He either knows something or he doesn't. I think it improper to expect this witness to assess the accuracy of these documents. What he can give us is his opinion, but he can't be expected to judge these documents as an expert.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry. If you don't -- I mean -- I think this is the same question that the Chamber put to him with respect to two documents, and it's -- all I'm asking is who would know better? Him, based on his on-site report, or the bomb squad expert report would be more determinative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. In light of the experience that he has had, I think he's able to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You started to answer the question. But if you could answer the question, which would prevail of those reports?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the aggregate report is an internal document for police purposes, and the other two reports are actually submitted to a Court; the expert analysis, the photo files, and the on-site investigation report. I would be hard put to say which is the most important one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But would you be able to say which one is more reliable or more determinative; your on-site report or the bomb squad expert report?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in my opinion, it would be my report, the report that I produced at the actual site.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would just state that it is our position that the issue of the direction or origin is less or perhaps not even at all important with respect to air bombs because of our position that -- that only the Bosnian Serb army had these weapons, so that must have been fired from the Bosnian Serb army positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's your submission. It would remain for the Chamber to access that in light of the all of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is something from the indictment, what my learned friend has just said. The trial will answer that question. I'm grateful for the opportunity to examine this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, sir, I represent the accused in this trial, and I would like to ask you something about the previous question raised by Mr. Whiting. Normally, you would arrive at the scene the next day after the incident, right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In this case, it was the next day after the incident that I arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What could you possibly have established the next day? Whoever had been injured had already been taken away, so what exactly did do you?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I photographed the scene, and we gathered any evidence found at the scene. The sites would normally be cordoned off by the police before we got there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So the police would wait for you to arrive. They would guard the site throughout the night. The next day you would be there to give your opinion; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I hope you heard this. The witness has just confirmed that the police would guard the scene throughout the night. The next day he would arrive and establish the facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What about those who were at the scene when the incident occurred and who looked after whoever had been injured? Were there any injured persons in this incident?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, three.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just injured, not dead?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The injuries were not serious, were they?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: My learned friend, Mr. Whiting, dealt with this a while ago. Did you ever see this sort of bomb actually fly?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Does it have a slow flight? Does it make much noise?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a lot of noise.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How long does it normally travel for?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I would be speculating.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, it's the noise that draws attention to the bomb. The flight itself is slow, so whoever is looking can get away from there and go somewhere safe, has plenty of time to do that, right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I assume that that would be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I wasn't going to ask you any questions about your statements. I'm not going to be using the first one, the one that you made in 1995. There's the other statement, too, dated the 15th of November, 1995. The document number is DD00-0673. This is your own statement dated the 15th of November, 1995. I have some questions in relation to this, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the document could please be placed before you, I would like to start with page 2. That's the one. I want page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is that your statement, sir? There, Witness, sir, paragraph 2. It reads: "I started on the six-month training course learning about forensic techniques, ballistics, biology, chemistry, and criminal law." You actually managed to master all these sciences over those six months, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't master all these skills in sciences. Those were just very basic lectures that we were supposed to use while carrying out on-site investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You decided to take up this very serious work, responsible work, should I say, which is to ascertain the circumstances under which a person was killed. After that, you would normally provide your opinion. Did you feel sufficiently qualified to do something like that, sir?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I can tell, you go on to state this: "I also attended lectures in photograph, making sketches, and taking fingerprints, investigation techniques raging from traffic accidents up to murder." Did you do that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did all of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember how many Serbs were murdered back in 1992, Serbs but also Croats and Bosnian who were killed; not on account of the war, but rather were slaughtered or shot?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact figure. Back in 1992, I wasn't working with the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But you did hear about that, right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If we read on you will see this: You talk about dealing with snipers. That's several paragraphs down. If there is a fatal shooting, can you see that section, sir?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If someone was shot dead, you assumed that those persons were killed by a sniper, right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand exactly what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This reads, "There is a fatal shooting if someone is shot dead." Can you explain to the Chamber what exactly you meant by that when you said this?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant, generally speaking, any on-site investigation where there was gun-fire that resulted in fatalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Even in cases of the an exchange of fire from both sides?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, even in those cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I won't be pursuing this any further. I would just be repeating myself. You did speak of another incident involving a tram. It's the second-to-last paragraph, same statement. You say,. "We also ascertained that the bullet had hit a -- the metal coated- plated radiator to keep people from burning themselves. When the bullet hit the other piece of metal, it must have shattered into pieces. Bits of the bullet and the metal protective layer of the radiator then hit passengers on that tram." Did you take that also to be a result of an exchange of fire, sir? ?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So you think it was a sniper, right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If indeed this was a sniper, how come he hit the radiator with the bullet fragmenting into three bits? He used just one bullet to virtually wound three different persons, right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is exactly what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The next paragraph, or rather, two paragraphs down the page, about the same incident. "The confrontation line at the site of this firing was only about 200 metres away." This is page 3, paragraph 2 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says, "about 200." That's what the B/C/S says.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: 200, about 200. Well, yes, excuse me. I know the language, too. You go on to say: "Our investigation was based on eye-witness information." Right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Including those who came to grief, right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did the victims tell you how they were injured and where from?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They made statements to my workmates, my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Even as soon as they were injured, they knew where they had been hit from, right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I assumed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In the second-to-last paragraph, you say in most of your reports, the bullets came from a southerly direction from the Metalka building; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So that the witness invariably said to you, that the bullets had come from the Metalka building, from that general direction?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. The first thing I would like to do is to tender this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, maybe it will be clarified if this is tendered, but I think that it misstates what is said in the second-to-last paragraph. It doesn't say that most of the bullets came from the Metalka building. It says "that this bullet," and it's talking about a particular incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. It says: "We were able to establish that this bullet came from the south, from the Metalka building, which is on the Serb side."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But I'm happy to have the -- if he's going to exhibit the statement, that's fine. It will be clear then on the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, please. That's what he said; and then I asked him about all of the sniping incidents that he was aware of. The bullet would invariably come from the Metalka building, and the witness said, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Were you then quoting from the statement, or were you simply putting a question to him?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I asked this question about -- we ascertained in relation to one bullet from the south from the Metalka building, and he said, yes; and then I asked, What about all the incidents that you were involved in? Did you always establish that the bullet, came from the Metalka building? And the witness said, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the direction of Grbavica, and I thought you were talking about this incident in particular.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. A while ago, you said, yes, but I'm still happy.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- counsel is misstating the record, again. It is page 44, line 17. The question that he put to the witness was: "In the second-to-last paragraph, you say in most of your reports the bullets came from a southerly direction, from the Metalka building; is that right? And that misstates what's in the report, and so, of course, the witness thought he was talking about this incident, which is what is being discussed in this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you for the clarification. Proceed, Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I won't be returning to that. That was my question, and I'll leave it at that. Just fort transcript following my learned friend's intervention, we would like to have this admitted DD00-0696 -- I apologise, that's not the right number. I was moving on to a difficult different one DD00-0673, the 15th of November.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, it's admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D60, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] .

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, this other statement that you made on the 17th of May, 2006, this is DD00-0696. Can we please have a look. Is that your statement, sir?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please now go to page 2? Just to gain time, in item 3, you talk about the Holiday Inn. You were answering a question by the Prosecutor. I won't be reading this back to you, but you said here: "We didn't know where the sniper was shooting from. It was foggy, and there were bullets whizzing past all around us." Is that an accuracy quote? Is that what you said, sir?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what the statement says. One thing I forgot to emphasise was the fact that the bullets were again arriving from the direction of Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Okay. You were born in Sarajevo, right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
