utterances.text: The very heart of Sarajevo lies in a valley. When the weather is foggy, it's impossible to actually see the bottom of the town from the hills around or the house tops?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't quite that foggy. It would have been sufficiently visible from the tops of the surrounding buildings, maybe not from these surrounding hills.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So this was a foggy day; we agree on that. Even so, you knew where the bullets were coming from. Who told you? Was that your own conclusion?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was our own conclusion where we were being fired at from. We concluded where the firing was coming from. We could hear the bullets.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Item number 7 -- it's not normal for me not to have any of my parents left, and I would like to express my sympathy to you because your father was killed. Here it reads: "My father was killed by a shell in 1992. He was off to fetch some water; and on his way back, he was killed right in front of the building." Did you give the investigator any sort of document for them to see to be able to tell whether that was, in fact, accurate whether your father was, indeed, killed by a shell, or perhaps there was a different reason is. It could have been a natural death, for all I know. Life can end in all sorts of ways. Was your father a soldier?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you have a document that shows cause of death?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't have it on me though.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You're both proceeding too fast. And if you look at the screen, you'll see that the interpreter is asking you to slow down. Observe a pause between question and answer. And, Mr. Tapuskovic, do not put three or four questions at the same time. One question at a time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] .

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you submit that document to the court so that we might be able to ascertain the cause of your father's death, sir?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I could. Although, the doctor who wrote the finding, Ilijas Dobreca, also died recently. If that means anything, I saw his dead body. I saw the wounds caused by shrapnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry the doctor died. What I'm asking you is whether you have this document and whether the document can be obtained from this medical institution in which your father's death was established?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that would be possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. When such investigations are at hand, such that you conducted in Sarajevo, was there a single case that you were involved in that included the most confident report which is one of the investigating judge?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There should be. An on-site investigation involves usually an investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it anywhere among the documents that we have discussed recently?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that one report quotes that a investigation judge was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I put it to you that the investigating judge was not there in a single incident?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you show me a document that shows that an investigating judge was on the spot?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not here.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was there a single military expert who knows about weapons who assisted you in your investigation at any point; not necessarily in uniform, but maybe in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some involved in the Cobanija incident, but they were observers.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you spoke about the events in Sarajevo and especially about the period of the summer of 1995, which was the worst for Sarajevo. Do you know that this coincided with a fierce offensive of the ABiH against the positions of army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know there was a lot of shooting, but who exactly was attacking --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You were working in the police?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How many policemen were there, 15.000, 20.000?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were they all under arms?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, policemen carry weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And that includes you?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had a pistol.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: How about that time and generally throughout those events in Sarajevo and around Sarajevo throughout the war, were you sometimes under the command of the army and were you involved there military operations?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war, the police did take part in military operations; in fact, it was the only armed force that existed at the very beginning of the war in 1992 and 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And later you dealt only with --

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I personally was never involved with military operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that other people were involved in military operations precisely in that year in the summer?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show the document DD00-0725, dated 6th July 1995. It's a very brief document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And you, Witness, will either confirm it or refute it when I show it to you. It would be even better if you could read it slowly.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean aloud?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, with the leave of the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is he to read, a particular paragraph or the entire document?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can read it to facilitate things. It says: "Command of the 12th Division. Sarajevo, 6th July, 1995." Is that correct.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: On the right-hand side, we see, "Defence of the Republik, Military Secret, Strictly Confidential." Correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "Engagement of MUP units in the defence of the city of Sarajevo. Order." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "In keeping with the current situation on the battlefield and the engagement of the units of the 1st Corps, and in keeping with the agreement of the commander of the Main Staff of the army and the Minister of the Internal Affairs of the 2nd July, 1995, for the purposes of efficiently defending the city of Sarajevo, and its airport as a vital facilitate for the city, and pursuant to the order of General staff of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina," number so-and-so, "I hereby order, one, continue to engage MUP units in the zone of responsibility of the 155th, 102nd, and 105th Mountain Brigades and the 111th Mountain Brigade and use them to defend and secure the area of responsibility of brigades and the airport as a vital facility for the city of Sarajevo." Are you aware of that document?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I am not going to deal with this document which is a bit longer, but it makes the same point?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's an order. If can you only look at one paragraph, and I would like to tender the previous document as a Defence Exhibit DD00-0725, with the leave of the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D61, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like DD00-0727. Here is another document, an order issued by Commander Prevljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the last page to see that this was indeed an order issued by is Commander Prevljak; it's on page 2?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was this signed by Prevljak?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it says, "Fikrat Prevljak."

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go back to page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Point 1.2. Is it correct that it reads: "Subheading, MUP units. MUP units and Lasta units from the current area of deployment, Butmir. Move to take up positions," et cetera, et cetera. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And another paragraph below. "From the forces of MUP detachments Bosna and Lasta, single out a reserve to the forces of Bosna detachment, one company strong." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what "Bosna" means?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a special unit of the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct to that this special unit of the police was involved in special assignment, special missions, such as sabotage?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So document DD00-0727 is a document I would like to tender.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to say I am a little bit baffled now about what the Rules are for getting the documents into evidence, because on direct examination this witness recognised medical documents pertaining to victims of an incident that he investigated. And it's -- and I submitted that at that was enough for it come into evidence, and the Defence objected and it was marked for identification. Now, he's being shown military documents he says he knows nothing about. He can't recognise and he can't comment on, and they're coming into evidence. I am happy to have -- my preference would be that these things come into evidence, and they are given whatever weight they should be given later by the Trial Chamber. I think that is the easiest way to do things. However, it seems to me that a consistent rule should apply with respect to documents. [Trial Chamber confers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. The general rule that we apply is that if the witness does not acknowledge the proposition put forward by the party, the document is not -- is not admitted. And the previous document will therefore not be admitted. That's the D61.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am tendering it to be marked for identification. It's a very long document containing a lot of things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we can mark it or identification. [Trial Chamber and registrar confer].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This document will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have document DD00-0725, which was admitted as Exhibit D61, will now not be admitted and will be marked for identification as D61. Document DD00-0727 will be marked for identification as Exhibit D62.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I omitted to mention it before, but the statement of this witness, DD00-07 -- 0673, on 15th November is another document I would like to tender.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you put that to the witness? D60, the 15th of November, we have already admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's probably my own fault. What I meant is the 17th May statement, 0696.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: What is that document?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the witness's statement that I questioned him on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, the witness's statement will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D63, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to ask the witness, since he spoke a lot about sniping, whether the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and primarily the MUP of Sarajevo had their own snipers and whether they fired on civilians within the city of Sarajevo or not.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you just repeat the last part?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Since you spoke a lot about snipers, were there any men among the MUP personnel who fired from tall buildings and sniper emplacements within the city of Sarajevo on targets within the city?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were there men in the military, in the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina who did that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not that I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Were there any sniping units?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean a special unit consisting of snipers? No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have document DD00-0723, dated 19th September, 1995. I would like to show this document to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you see this order? It's an order dated the 19th of September signed, again, by Commander Fikret Prevljak?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, I will read it to you very slowly. "Pursuant to the order by the commander of the 1st Corps, strictly confidential," number such-and-such, "and based on certain information gained by the UNPROFOR in the territory of Sarajevo, sniping activities of our units is very strong. And in this connection, the attention of the President of the Presidency has been drawn and a protest addressed seeking immediate succession of these activities." Is that written there?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was it during the NATO bombing, the date as you see it, the 19th of September?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you exactly in which period the NATO bombing took place, but it was around that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And what is this order about? "One, immediately stop fire from all sorts of weapons, especially snipers." Is that written there?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: There is no need for me to read the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like this document DD00-0723 to be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This will be marked for identification as D64.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I now have two documents that I was reprimanded about by the Prosecutor, and I received them from the Prosecutor himself two years ago, probably as a potential Prosecution exhibit. In any case, I'm going to show this document, which is 65 ter 01989. It is dated 27th August 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see this document, Witness?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I see it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This document is, again, signed by the then commander of the 1st Corps, Mr. Karavelic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It has its own reference number, and Karavelic is writing to the minister, Dr. Hasan Muratovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It reads: "Mr. Minister, further to your letter number 01-021-525, dated 25th August, 1994, I hereby wish to advise you as follows." Next paragraph: "In the building of the executive council, there are no units of the 1st Corps or snipers belonging to our force. The building of the executive council is secured and guarded by the MUP with their own personnel." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "The said incident was notified by General Soubirou to Mr. Enes Bezdrov, Chief of Security Services Centre, CSB, and we believe these incidents will be avoided in the future. As for the freedom of movement of the UNPROFOR in Radnica, Butmir, and Zokolovic colony, we took appropriate action; in short, complete freedom of movement." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Is it the case that there were MUP snipers on top of this very tall building, the building of the executive council, and hereby Karavelic is refuting his own responsibility and is assuring the minister that this building is not used as an emplacement of MUP snipers?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you anything about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 01989, I would like to tender this, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think it's also marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be marked for identification as D65.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, can the witness please be shown a document that has been in the possession of the OTP for a long time. It's DD00-0681. DD00-0681.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see the document, sir?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not yet -- right, it's there. All right. But needs to be blown up slightly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Same thing I was about to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please. There.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You see just below the line, I won't be tiring the Chamber with the header, that reads, "The Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, President of the Presidency." You see that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Just below that, it says, "Greetings, Izetbegovic," at the bottom of the document, right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, here, I'll read it to you. Alija Izetbegovic is writing to General Delic, the commander of the General of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that right.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "General, this morning the French ambassador, Henri Jacquolin, visited my office and told my advisor, Mamija, this among other things. France would like to make it official known that we have very angry because of the murder of one of our soldiers at Dobrinja. Military expertise had shown that the soldier had been hit from a positions held by the Bosnian army, and yet we have not had an opportunity to check this, which means that we can only have suspicions." Is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "The Chetniks, in this case, have demonstrated endless cooperation and willingness to cooperation by making it possible to UN investigators to enter each and every flat and each and every position along the line held by them." Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "Our men, on the other hand, have refused any form of cooperation and have not allowed access to them to any of the numerous locations from which the French soldier could have been hit." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: He stated, "When the BH army allows the UNPROFOR commission access to the buildings from which the bullet could have been fired at the French soldier, it is only then that we willing able to discuss the normalisation of relations between Paris and Sarajevo." Is that right.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "The French ambassador has caused us an unpleasant surprise by saying that he had proof that the out of the 24 French soldiers killed, who were members of the UN, not taking into account those who were killed in the traffic accident at Igman, more than half of those had been killed by the BH army." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: He says that, "General Gobillard complained to him that for weeks our commanders had been ruling out each and every contact with UNPROFOR. "We don't understand your behaviour, and we don't see what you are trying to achieve." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "Of course, some of these allegations must be taken with a pinch of salt. But it's also necessary for you to know what their objections are. Remove any obstacles to cooperation wherever no obstacles are necessary from the military point of view. Sarajevo, the 21st of April, 1995, Salam Alija Izetbegovic." Is my reading accurate, sir?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can I have this document admitted as a Defence exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all, I think would be marked for identification, but I would raise a larger issue about what the point of this cross-examination is. This is a policeman, and he's repeatedly been shown military documents and their being read out to him. And now counsel is even abandoned even asking him if he knows anything about it. He just reads it out and then tries to move it into evidence. There is no indication that this witness knows anything about military documents, and that he is going to be of any assistance of these document. And I can tell you, judging from the list, there are a lot more of these.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I'm asking you counsel also in the same vein, why are you seeking to introduce these documents through this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I was about to show you why, and this is the very reason I decided to do it through this witness. I would like you to at least mark this for identification. The Prosecution have been in the possession of this document for years. Perhaps not from the date the document was produced, but certainly from sometime after. I'm about to tell you why I'm showing these document to the witness. He says there was no sniping by the MUP that transpires with great clarity from everything that we have been reading, and I will be asking some questions that will shed more light on the entire problem. Mr. Whiting knows about these documents that I'm about to show; he's seen them before. It's his right, I suppose. Perhaps he can stop me from showing these documents. Perhaps it's a right that he has. He was talking a while ago about the position that the Prosecution being jeopardised. The only thing that I see is the possibility that the position of this accused might be jeopardised when discussing this effort; whereas, Mr. Whiting a while ago talked about the Prosecution being jeopardised. I couldn't understand that. The question is through my cross-examination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one moment, please. [Trial Chamber confers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So far, all the witness has done is to confirm the -- that what you have read is actually in the report. He hasn't spoken to the contents of the report, and the -- what the Chamber will do is to mark it for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D66, Your Honour -- sorry, marked for identification as D66, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with your ruling. He says that the MUP or anyone from MUP never fired at civilians in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, please continue with your cross-examination instead of rehearsing what we have done.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, are you familiar with the incident on the 25th of October, 1994 at about 1800 hours, the medical institute. Eight passengers from that tram were admitted. The tram was fired from the PZT Grbavica near the Brotherhood and Unity bridge. Eight people were hit?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about that incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You don't, fair enough. What about this report? It's a report compiled by one of your colleagues dated the 25th of October. I will read it to you just to see whether -- or if you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: My objection is that this report was on the list of exhibits, documents that the -- that Defence was going to use. It was on the list that they provided yesterday, and it was dropped from the list that they provided to me today. So I don't understand how counsel is about to use it, particularly in the manner that he is using it. The witness has said he doesn't know anything about it, and now he is just going to try to read from the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me ascertain from Mr. Tapuskovic, did you drop it from your list, the list of the documents that you would be using in your cross-examination? Just now please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would never have dropped it. I submitted it in good time. It was disclosed to the OTP at the right time, and there was no way I could have dropped it. The OTP got it the moment the present witness took the oath. Now, as to why the e-court system works the way it does sometimes, that is not my problem. I don't know about technology, but the OTP got the document the moment this witness took his oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Listen, I really don't want to spend a lot of time on this, but I'm just going to ask Mr. Whiting if he can very quickly verify what he has said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: According to my information, that is not correct. It's document 435, I believe, and it's not on the spreadsheet that was provided to me today, which I -- I don't know if that spreadsheet was provided to the court, but today I received it -- I received a spreadsheet today with the documents that were going to be used, and it's not on there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's on the --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's on the list for yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's on the list for the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It was on the list that was provided yesterday. [Trial Chamber confers].

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I have the list from today; it's right here. I'm happy to provide it to the Chamber. It has markings on it, but it was not on the list provided to me today. And I think counsel probably knows that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, did you provide a list, today, of the documents that you are going to use to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would be crazy. I would be crazy to do that and break the rules that we have agreed on. That's impossible. Mr. Whiting has been smothering me in e-mail since yesterday. I stopped answering. He has been drawing me to certain things trying to hamstring me in my cross-examination. Why would I do it today? It's machine of been in e-court for at least two or three days. What do I know? I must have submitted that document at least two or three days ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, please pass the document to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The document I'm passing up, and if Defence counsel wants to see it first, it's a printout of the e-mail that I received this morning and the attached spreadsheet. There are markings that I made on the spreadsheet. [Trial Chamber confers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm just going to ask -- I think we're wasting time, but I'm going to ask the usher to show this document to the Defence. This is the document that Mr. Whiting has passed to us. Mr. Whiting says that is a document which you transmitted today, and it doesn't have this -- a reference to this particular document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I sent the entire batch I have been showing you about Izetbegovic and all that. It was all at the same time. I can't be looking at these all the time. It's what I have my associates for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The document that is in your hand that I just sent to you, did you transmit it to the Prosecutor today?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, no way. You might as well arrest me. I'll give up my job. Please arrest me in that case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm not going to spend any more time on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, the confusion may be that it came from the case manager. It did not come obviously from Mr. Tapuskovic itself. It came from the case manager, and I believe they can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Did you or your case manager send it. Because if your case manager sent it, she is sending it on your behalf.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't shift the blame to my case manager. It's my responsibility. If anybody is to be called to account, it is going to be me. But I submitted this along with the Izetbegovic document. What is happening with e-court? Why is it so late in opening documents sometimes. I'm going into that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Find out from your case manager right now. Find out from your case manager whether she sent that document to Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yesterday, but there must have been a problem with the e-court system for that to be submitted. We looked at that document yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You haven't answered the question. Did she send it to the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes. I have been saying that all along, haven't I? [Trial Chamber confers].

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everything has been fair so far. You submit the documents to us on the same day that were going to be used, and we weren't angry with you or anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We are not allowing you to use it in accordance with the rules that we established. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mean, Your Honours, this will crop up with the next witness anyway. This hurdle shall be easier for me to overcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know this, Witness, what about the UNPROFOR report drafted by the French generals? Did they not say that nearby buildings were fired at by members of the BiH army? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I see this other document. I wonder if I submitted this one in good time. This is 65 ter 1484. D19; one of ours. It runs into quite a number of pages. I will be showing only two of those. Page 203, official report, dated 19th of November, 1994. A number of your colleagues produced this report. This is a set of documents. 65 ter 1484 starts with 199, and what I'm talking about is at 203. It's an official report. Three pages on from here--

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: For assistance, the English of that page is RR25-1202 to RR25-1204.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The B/C/S is 251203.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, it appears that multiple translations of this document were submitted. There are four in the system, and we're having a hard time figuring out which one goes with the B/C/S/.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, that is why I tried to help. It's the one that is 1202 to 1204 that pertains to these pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] .

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you see this official report dated 19th November regarding an incident where that boy was hurt. You heard about that? Do you know about that boy who was killed and his mother was wounded. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can't remember this particular incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The whole world heard about it.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember. I just can't recall it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This is a large paragraph, a large one, a small one, then a large one and the end. "On the pavement of the -- on the Franje Rackog Street, there were no UNPROFOR vehicles. Soon two APCs of the French battalion UNPROFOR came and parked with license numbers, UN-PF 15225 and 15041." Can you see that? And then it goes on to say: "Other witnesses, other eye-witnesses, were not found. On the spot where the woman and boy were injured, there was a bloodstain that UNPROFOR members who later came to the site washed out with water and covered with soil before the on-site investigation team arrived." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Since the Frenchmen were most correct in conducting these investigations, were they a particular favourite target of the members of your units?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you anything about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, where is this line of cross-examination taking us, and what is the -- what is its relevance?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The relevance lies in the fact that this evidence indicates that UNPROFOR soldiers, at the time when this commander was the commander, were being killed by members of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the MUP of Sarajevo, and the blame was always laid in the eyes of the world on Serb units. That is precisely why the document issued by the man who then led the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Mr. Alija Izetbegovic, invokes the fact that he was informed by the French ambassador that 12 French soldiers were killed by the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, precisely because the Frenchmen were the most diligent their on-site investigations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I hear that. But can you relate that specifically to the criminal responsibility of the accused? Are you asking us to draw a particular inference from that as to his liability or non-liability; and if so, what would that be?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The point I'm trying to make is that not a single bullet was ever fired from the positions of the army of Republika Srpska at the UNPROFOR or at a child with a conscious intention to kill the child or a member of the UNPROFOR. Such things could have happened only as part of a major offensive, the major offensive conducted at the time by the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that is in line with this witness said about the summer of 1995 being the worst. It is my belief, and I don't know whether you will share this belief, that this is very relevant because it allows us to determine that the UNPROFOR was never allowed to investigate properly the murders of -- the killings of UNPROFOR soldiers because it would have been easy to see through the deceit that it was the Serb units who did it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The next issue is whether this witness is in a position to assist you, even assuming that you are correct in what you just said. The witness so far has not been able to confirm anything in any of these reports. He simply confirms what you have read.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I did not even expect him to be able to confirm something like that. He contested that anybody ever from the police force fired from those sky-scrapers. And even when I showed him that letter from Muratovic, I knew that I would get a negative answer. But a document speaks for itself and I will use the documents for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: If you know from before that the witness can't confirm anything in it, why are you putting it to him? Because the most we can do is marked for identification. Wait there is a witness through whom you can properly put it into evidence, or if you have a witness on your list when the accused presents his case, then that would be an appropriate time. But I have to consider with my colleagues whether to allow this kind of questioning to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more word, Your Honour, and then you will decide. That document that contained the relevant information, I was stopped from using that document base Mr. Whiting knew very well that the witness was involved where those eight people were injured in that tram. He was involved as an investigator and, of course, I was not allowed by the Prosecution to pursue it. I will try to use the same document through another witness. It is up to you to decide how to proceed now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, I'm not going to allow further questioning of this witness in relation to this document. He has no relationship with it. It's not taking us any further. I would, however, wish to see the document which we -- which we disallowed on the basis that you had not notified the Prosecutor that you were going to us it, and that is because you say that it has evidence that is related to this witness. And we would consider allowing you to cross-examine on it, if that is the case. So would you transmit that document to us that we can have a look at it. That is the document which you say this witness knows about, because he -- he knows about the -- he was investigating the tram incident in which eight persons were injured. But shouldn't that have been provided to the Chamber as well? Is this the document on the -- on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, I did not take with me the entire document, but I will read it. It's part of a very large document that relates to the wounding of those women.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us be clear what you're going to do. Is there a translation of that document?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Maybe the Prosecution has a translation. I believe they do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a 65 ter document, 648.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is -- this page is part of a larger document which is 65 ter number 648. We do not have a translation of this page or any other page in that substantial document. This particular page, as far as I can tell, as far as I was able to determine before I abandoned any further inquiry on this because I thought it was being dropped, this particular page does not relate to the witness. There are other indications in this larger document that the witness may have been involved in the investigation. But what is at issue involved in this particular page, as far as I can tell, does in the relate to the witness. And this is the one page that Defence counsel indicated that he wanted to use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let us be clear, Mr. Tapuskovic, the Chamber will allow to you cross-examine on this document to the extent that the witness knows about the contents, and it's only on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you just heard from the Prosecutor. He was part of the team who worked on the substantial document. He was on that team. I cannot say what he will state. The Prosecutor himself says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Let us hear the cross-examination on those parts of the document to which the witness can speak on the basis of his experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I put it to the witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It is not the very legible. It's an Official Note drafted on 26th October 1994 on the premises of the Security Services Sarajevo, after attending a site where a street car was fired on, on 25th October 1994 around 1700 hours at the intersection of Vojvode Putnika and Sibenska streets. I'm reading on: "On the 26th of October, 1994, around 1715 hours, I attended a site on Vojvode Putnika Street, and my assignment was to observe the work of the UNPROFOR commission who were tasked with inspecting the scene and the tram and determine on that basis where the fire had come from. When I came to the site, I found three members of the UNPROFOR of the French battalion."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is that the first paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's all of the document. This is the entire document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "The tram was facing Cengic Vila. The distance between the back of the tram and the tram depot of Pofalici was around 15 metres. At that moment, representatives of the UNPROFOR exited from the tram and passed on its left side in the direction of movement. On that side of the tram, there were clear signs of damage of the body of the tram inflicted by infantry weapons. An UNPROFOR officer pushed a metal bar into one of the holes and said something to those present in the French language. "Other members of the team did not do or say anything. My interpreter told me that the officer had said that the shots had come from the Muslim side from a neighbouring white building in Sibenska Street. The interpreter said that the officer was even able to establish the window from which the shots came from. After noting this, the officer took out the metal bars and together with his team left the site around 1745 hours. The driver of the tram took the tram to the depot." Now my question is, since this Official Note was signed by Sulejman Pilav, were you indeed the member of -- a member of that team?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had more questions, but I'm not going to proceed with them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just have a few questions, but I don't recall when the next break is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Oh, it's now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Oh, it's now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We'll take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Before you begin, Mr. Whiting, I need to clarify something with Mr. Tapuskovic. It was document 435. It was document 435, which was the subject of a dispute between yourself and the Prosecutor as to whether you had given the proper notification that you were going to use it, and that is the document which I said I would allow -- listen it to me first. That is the document that I said I would allow you to cross-examine on, notwithstanding the fact that the Chamber had earlier disallowed it in accordance it the rules that we had established, because you had not notified the Prosecutor of it in the -- in your communication to him today, the communication that came from your court manager. But it's not clear to me whether that was the document which you most laterally put to the witness. That's the document you wanted to cross-examine on, and I said yes, because you said there was a reference to a tram incident in which eight persons were killed and this witness had investigated it. Is that the document which you put to the witness? Because it does not appear to me to have been that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Eight persons were wounded, and that's this entire document that I did not bring with me. I have only a part thereof. And what the UNPROFOR did on site had to do precisely with that tram hit with eight rounds, and the UNPROFOR established it was from the positions of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, just a minute. Didn't you say that this witness could assist you on that, that you had questions to put to this witness about that document? You were fighting to have that document, struggling to have it used by you in court, and I allowed you to use it. But it seems to me that have you not used it, and I want to know why.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, when he confirmed that what is written in that report is possible, that it was fire coming from that building where the ABiH positions were, that was sufficient to me. I thought it was not necessary to burden you with it any longer. I just want that document exhibited, and I forgot to tender it. I didn't see any reason to question him any longer, if he confirmed that it was indeed a possibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you for the clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is not my understanding of the record. The question that was put to the witness was not "was what is stated in the report possible." "It was were you a member of that team," and the answer was "possibly." That was the only question that was put to him. I don't think that he confirmed in any way, even that it was possible what was stated in that document. Now, you know, as I said before, this document is a page from a longer report that deals with this incident. It's 65 ter 648; and if counsel wants to show that bigger document, even though it was not on their list, in the spirit of cooperation, which may be needed today, I'm happy to allow that. Of course, it's up to the Chamber to make that decision. I wouldn't have any objection. It's a long document for which there is no translation, and it's obviously a complicated issue. There are ins and outs of this issue, as far as I can tell, based on the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Can I just ask a question: What happened to document 65 ter number 435?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That is not -- it's not 65 ter 435; that's the Defence number 435, so it's not a 65 ter number from our list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: So we are speaking about one and the same document then.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The document that Defence counsel wanted to use is 435. It is the one that he showed it to the witness. He read it to the witness and asked that single question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have already said what I meant. I thought he said it's possible, and he worked on the team. I can continue, but you did not allow me to use document DD00-0432, from which it transpires that it was something that happened a day earlier, on the 235th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And that document lists the persons who were injured, and you were in the team that tried to elucidate that case, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would you like to put additional questions to him about 435?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You said a moment ago that it is possible that what is written in the document is true?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not what you asked me. You asked me whether Sulejman Pilav, who signed the document, was in my team and I said it was possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The team that elucidated that case?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I didn't confirm the allegations from that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't ask you to confirm the allegations from that document. I asked you to confirm that it was done by your team, because you never worked alone?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So whatever the team did together is the definitive position of that team?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That was my understanding. So you were familiar with the whole documentation of that case?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, with a proviso that this does not relate to the case itself. It relates to what happened during the on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But that document that I read out to you, it is directly related to the event from the day before because this document was drafted after the UNPROFOR attended the scene on the 26th?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is one Official Note with just notes that the UNPROFOR attended and made a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And it's in the framework of your team?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It is not one of the findings from the on-site investigation, and it was not written by the crime technician who did the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: It is mentioned in several places in that document that your team does not agree with what is stated?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Whiting --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I suggest that the entire document be exhibited. The Prosecutor knows the number of the entire document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: 65 ter 648. I have no objection to that, the whole thing going in. It will have to be translated. It's a -- but that's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, it will very burdensome and, in fact, would be a waste of resources to have the whole thing translated if, in fact, you're only concerned with a particular portion of it. So if you can identify the particular portion that is relevant, we'll admit it and we'll have that portion translated. But to ask the translators to translate, what is it, 600 pages --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, if I was not clear. It's not 600 pages. It looks like about 38 pages. I think probably it would be prudent just to get it done because I think Defence counsel may be interested in certain parts and, we may be interested in certain parts. This may become an issue with other witnesses. Rather than do this piecemeal, I think the whole thing is important for the Trial Chamber to have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. If it's 38 pages, we will admit it and it will be translated.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D67, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: This is re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. Could I have Exhibit D60 on the screen, please, and if we could look at page 3 in both the B/C/S and the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, do you see the paragraph, the second paragraph in the B/C/S. I'm just going to ask you to read that paragraph until the end of the document; and when you're done, I'm going to ask you if you can confirm what's stated there is accurate. While you're reading, however, I do want to, in fairness, signal to the Trial Chamber and to the Defence that this -- what's contained in that part of the statement, which the Defence has put into evidence, pertains to sniping incident number 9, which is an incident that we dropped in December. So it is -- it falls into that category of dropped incidents. I did not lead evidence on it, following the Trial Chamber's ruling on this issue. However, I think now the Defence has opened the door to this, by putting in this statement; and in fairness, I think I should be permitted simply to ask him if he can confirm the accuracy of what is in this statement pertaining to this issue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would you explain what you moan by "dropped."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What I mean is that we -- as you will recall, the original indictment had a certain number of scheduled incidents; and pursuant to the Trial Chamber's order at the beginning of December last year, we were ordered to cut the case by a third and we dropped certain scheduled incidents. Later on the Trial Chamber held that we could not lead any evidence; but pertaining to those dropped incidents, we have filed a motion asking for a modification of the Trial Chamber's order in that regard, allowing us to lead some evidence on that issue. The Defence has not yet responded to that motion and, of course, the Trial Chamber has the not ruled on it; and for that reason, I did not lead any evidence on this issue. But, as I said, now I think the door has been open to it. The Defence put the statement into evidence, so I think I should permitted to ask him if he can confirm, and that's all, I won't take it any further, but if he can confirm what is written there in his statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, you may do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, have you had an opportunity to read from that second paragraph till the end of the statement?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And is what's written in those paragraphs accurate, to the best of your knowledge; true and accurate, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Could I now look at Defence exhibit number 63, which is the other statement of the witness, and if we could go to the second page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If you could look at paragraph 3 and just read paragraph 3 for me, and I'll just have one or two questions about it.

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In the sentence before the last sentence, where it says "the bullets were zipping past us from across the Miljacka river," can you tell us what -- from this position where you were at the National Restaurant, what is located, what neighbourhood is located across the Miljacka river?

utterances.speaker: BOGDAN VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Grbavica neighbourhood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, that concludes your evidence. We thank you for giving it, and you may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The next witness will be handled by Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour the next witness is Mr. Butt, and might we have a bit of time to manoeuver.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I be excused just for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may seat, and you may begin, Mr. Sachdeva.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Butt.

utterances.speaker: ASAM BUTT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I'm just going to ask some questions about your personal background.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Mr. President, with your leave, may I lead the witness through these issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Butt, it's correct that you retired from the Pakistani army in 2005?

utterances.speaker: ASAM BUTT
utterances.text: Yes. I retired from Pakistani army as a lieutenant-colonel in October 2005.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you were a lieutenant-colonel, but you had that position with the emoluments of a brigadier; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ASAM BUTT
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You joined the Pakistani army in 1976?

utterances.speaker: ASAM BUTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And your speciality was in communications; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ASAM BUTT
utterances.text: Yes. I am an a telecommunication engineer and that was my speciality and I served in the code of signals of Pakistani army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, were you ever assigned to Liberia?

utterances.speaker: ASAM BUTT
utterances.text: I was assigned today UN Military Observer mission in Liberia. On 31st August, I left the country, 1994. And I was there for about five to six weeks. So I take it you joined towards the middle of July 1994; is that right.

utterances.speaker: ASAM BUTT
utterances.text: No. I left on 31st of August, the country for Liberia; and by 2nd or 3rd September, 1994, I was in Mondrovia then the capital of Liberia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Very well. You left Pakistan on the 31st of August. Well, firstly, why did you leave Liberia after six weeks?

utterances.speaker: ASAM BUTT
utterances.text: It was because of the deteriorating situation. We could not be declared there. It was decided a mission was curtailed, and then we were redeployed in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: When did you go to Bosnia and with whom?

utterances.speaker: ASAM BUTT
utterances.text: Yes. I along with other three to four UNMOs; a couple of them from Czechoslovakia and two from Pakistan. We came from Liberia to Bosnia via Amsterdam. I still remember that I left Monrovia on 10th of October, and on 11th of October I was in Zagreb, then the UNMO headquarters, Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So just to be clear, you went to Bosnia with the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: ASAM BUTT
utterances.text: Yes. Again, there I was assigned the duty of UN Military Observer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And when did you -- can you tell me -- tell the Court roughly when you arrived in Zagreb with the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: ASAM BUTT
utterances.text: It was 11th of October when I arrived in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: In Zagreb, did you undergo any training there?

utterances.speaker: ASAM BUTT
utterances.text: Yes, for about ten to 12 days, and after that I was sent to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: What kind of training did you undertake?

utterances.speaker: ASAM BUTT
utterances.text: It started from the introduction about our working deployment of United Nations, it's scenario; how we had to conduct an armoured routine, and some military training related to crater analysis. When I said the military training, it was not the physical training only, but practical training. What we were supposed to do during our tenure of duty with United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: When you say crater analysis, can you very briefly elaborate on that?

utterances.speaker: ASAM BUTT
utterances.text: Yes, we were shown -- a small little pamphlet was issued to us, and our instructor, a name I don't remember, trained us, instructed us how to carry out the crater analysis, and how to find the bearing of the weapon from where the fire came and where impact was created.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And these craters, the craters that were going to analyse, what were they caused from?

utterances.speaker: ASAM BUTT
utterances.text: Mostly, these were from the mortars and, of course, other projectiles we were also taught about.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And did the training cover the determination of the direction of fire?

utterances.speaker: ASAM BUTT
utterances.text: Yes. In bearing, we were taught to how to carry out -- how to find out direction of that mortar from where that fire came.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And is that, indeed, what you did when you arrived in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ASAM BUTT
utterances.text: Yes, mostly. As most of the time, we were busy about the impacts, so that knowledge and training was quite handy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: When you were posted to Sarajevo, did you join a particular team?

utterances.speaker: ASAM BUTT
utterances.text: Yes. It was the Mali Hum team, located just short of -- while travelling from Sarajevo town toward Mali Hum, a small mountain towards the north of the city, there was a communication tower, and just before that was our team location, which also had incidently the observation post in the same communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: For the benefit of the Court, I will show you a map and ask you to mark that location in a moment. But just tell me how many, if you know, how many UNMO teams were there in Sarajevo when you got there?

utterances.speaker: ASAM BUTT
utterances.text: There were about fire to six UNMOs once I joined them, but the strength varied from six to 12 UNMOs, sometimes there were five, six, sometime eight. It kept on changing during my tenure of duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, are you talking UNMOs per UNMO team or the total number of UNMOs in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ASAM BUTT
utterances.text: No. This was the strength I had talked about for my team, which was located at Mali Hum.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: How many UNMO teams were there in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ASAM BUTT
utterances.text: In Sarajevo, there was one team in Sedrenik; one was my own team; and there was another team for Novo Sarajevo. It was located close to us. Their accommodation was close us to, but their area of responsibility was towards the west of my area of responsibility; also a team in Hrasnica. Of course, there were -- my team was divided into two teams; one part was ours; and the other part was towards the Serb side and it was located in Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: That leads on to my next question. I wanted to ask you at the time that you arrived in Sarajevo, were there United Nations Military Observer in both the Bosnian government territory and the Bosnian Serb territory?

utterances.speaker: ASAM BUTT
utterances.text: Yes. There were military observers on both the sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Do you know how many teams there were in the Bosnian Serb territory?

utterances.speaker: ASAM BUTT
utterances.text: I know about other teams. I may not be remembering exactly. I Gradci and Zepa. Our teams were there. Also there observers teams for liaison purposes; we used to call it Lima. It was to carry out liaison with the Lukavica Barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So apart from Grbavica, the UNMO had a liaison officer in Lukavica Barracks; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ASAM BUTT
utterances.text: Not exactly in Lukavica Barracks because I never visited there so I cannot comment on that. But he was working as liaison officer from military observer side, and mostly he was interacting with Lukavica barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Do you know who that person mostly interacted with from the Lukavica Barracks?

utterances.speaker: ASAM BUTT
utterances.text: Yes. I know Mr. Indic, and probably it was Colonel Indic. But anyway, he was Mr. Indic who was being referred by our observer who was doing as -- as liaison officer from observer side towards the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And just to be clear, Colonel Indic, was he part of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: ASAM BUTT
utterances.text: I think he should be because it was a Romanija corps and the Serb side, which was taking care of Sarajevo. So it has to be part of that particular corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: You said that you were posted at Mali Hum. Did you on any occasion work on the Bosnian Serb side within the Sarajevo environs.

utterances.speaker: ASAM BUTT
utterances.text: No. But I still remember that on 27th February, I was, by my team leader, asked to go to the Serb side, where my other half of the team was located in Grbavica, as I had mentioned earlier, along with a Nigerian military observer, Major Odidi. We went there on 27th of February, reached team accommodation, and suddenly I received a message from our liaison observer from the Serb, Lima, that Mohammed, as I was referred to - my first name was Mohammed - must leave this Serb side. And these orders or instructions were from Mr. Colonel Indic; otherwise, he would be arrested. Soon after these instructions or orders, a Serb soldier was posted on the door of our accommodation and I was given two hours to leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Let me just stop you there. Firstly, actually in my haste to try and -- to increase the speed of the examination, I forgot to ask you to state your full name and your place of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: ASAM BUTT
utterances.text: Okay. I am Mohammed Asem Butt. I was born on 27th of September 1957 - and Butt is B-u-t-t - in a city in the Punjab state of Pakistan.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, you said you were asked by your team leader to go to the Serb side. Why were you asked to go to the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: ASAM BUTT
utterances.text: It was because on the Serb side, in our team, there was shortage of observers. So they said me and Odidi should go there and do duty for about seven to ten days, and later on we were to come back.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And when you got there, you have told the Court that you received a message from your liaison officer that you must leave. Do you know why you were told that?

utterances.speaker: ASAM BUTT
utterances.text: Then didn't give any reason, but they said Mohammed to leave and I was forced to leave. After about one hour, I went back to my team at Mali Hum. It was basically for the reason during my tenure of duty, it was my assessment, and that can be verified by the UN records of that time, Muslims were not welcomed on the Serb side as observer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And again, just to be clear, so you in fact did leave after two or three hours and went back to the Bosnian government side?

utterances.speaker: ASAM BUTT
utterances.text: Not two to three hours. After getting the confirmation from my UNMO headquarters, they also confirmed. And after that, I left the accommodation of Grbavica and started coming back towards my team. And, again, on my way to Mali Hum, at the Serb checkpoint, I was stopped and under went every kind of search, and kept on waiting. Again, they got some instructions from somebody, and only then I was allowed to go back or to cross over to the Bosnian side. Again, it took about one hour there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So, in total, how long had you attempted to carry out your work as an UNMO on the Bosnian Serb side.

utterances.speaker: ASAM BUTT
utterances.text: This was the only time. As an UNMO, I went there to my team side. But I still remember on a couple of times, I visited a couple of buildings in connection with some investigations along with French people.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Yes. I'm going to get to that in a moment, but I just want to stick to this one occasion. You said in February that you had gone to the Serb side. Just to be clear, did you, in fact, stay for the seven days in Grbavica?

utterances.speaker: ASAM BUTT
utterances.text: Not as per the instructions of Mr. Indic and the confirmation from the UNMO headquarters. I think it took about 45 minutes or one hour, and I left the accommodation and went through the Serb checkpoint, where I was searched, and stayed until the time they got instructions, and then they didn't allow me to cross over. But after about one hour, I was allowed to go and I then went back to Mali Hum; same day, after about one hour, 45 minutes stay in Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Now, generally in the work of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd just like to check witness. There were UNMOs on the Serbian side, not the whole team was sent back, you personally were because you said you were Muslim. Did I understand you rightly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was only me who was sent back, and Odidi who accompanied me to Grbavica stayed there and was not objected. It is my assessment that being a Muslim, I was not accepted there. The situation which was there then was that hardly any UNMO, at least I don't remember, was deployed on the Serb side because they were not accepted there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was a Nigerian major who wasn't a Muslim, was he?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was Christian from Nigeria and part of my team which was located at Mali Hum, and he along with me was supposed to stay for seven to ten days in Grbavica. However, once I was objected, I had to leave but he stayed in Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Mr. Butt, you said that this incident took place in February on the 27th of February. Was that in 1995?

utterances.speaker: ASAM BUTT
utterances.text: It was 1994 -- sorry, sorry. I correct myself. February was 1995, because I joined the mission in 1994. February, once I went to Grbavica, the year was 1995. I stand corrected. I'm sorry, Your Honour, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And you joined the mission in October 1994; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ASAM BUTT
utterances.text: That's correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Generally, in the work of an UN Military Observer, were there any principles or standards that you had to adhere to in discharging your duties?

utterances.speaker: ASAM BUTT
utterances.text: It was a total impartiality, irrespective of any religion, any nationality, any faction, any group. It was to be above all and for --

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Excuse me, sorry. Carry on.

utterances.speaker: ASAM BUTT
utterances.text: And for that, the standing operating procedure was -- the practice in vogue was that in any UNMO team, there would be no repetition of nationality. That means that if there is an UNMO in one of teams from one country, it would not be represented by a second UNMO; only one UNMO from one country. And whenever we used to go on parole or for some investigation, it had to be not one UNMO, at least two UNMOs, to ensure that it is carrying out investigations impartially.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: And the two UNMOs from that patrol team would be of different nationalities; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ASAM BUTT
utterances.text: That's true. Of course, it had to be from different nationalities because in one team, there couldn't be two UNMOs from one country.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: When you got to Sarajevo and when you were deployed to the Mali Hum team, what was your rank, if I may use that word.

utterances.speaker: ASAM BUTT
utterances.text: Then I was a major. I joined the mission as a major. And after I was dispatched from the mission in September of 1995, I was promoted as lieutenant-colonel. In fact, the news I got during my tenure of UN was that back home I had already been promoted?

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: Sorry. It was my question perhaps. Within the UNMO team itself, what role did you have when you joined?

utterances.speaker: ASAM BUTT
utterances.text: When I joined, as per the UN SOP of the mission, I joined as a member. And after three or four months, I became a member of the half of the team which was located in the Mali Hum, and later on a member of the entire team.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: So did you, in fact, become the team leader?

utterances.speaker: ASAM BUTT
utterances.text: Yes. I became team leader of half of the team which was located in Mali Hum. After about three or four months and after an additional another one to two months, I became team leader of the entire team, which was located as Mali Hum.

utterances.speaker: MR. SACHDEVA
utterances.text: I wanted to ask you about shelling and sniping within the period that you were in Sarajevo. Firstly, did you investigate sniping and shelling incidents involving civilian casualties?

utterances.speaker: ASAM BUTT
utterances.text: Yes. Quite a few shelling and sniping incidents I investigated, along with other UNMOs. These are numerous in numbers, and varied from -- it had, in fact, various weapons used. We had shelling of mortars of various calibre. We had shelling investigation of modified air bomb.
